title: Anchored Reserves with Scaled Surge Crediting — packaging, SLA bands, and negotiation playbook
creator: Anika Shah
body: Background: Enterprise customers increasingly want predictable unit economics for high-throughput inference while retaining the ability to absorb short-term spikes. Existing reserved GPU offers (flat commit + burst) either lock customers into large monthly spend or leave them exposed to availability preemption. Goal: Define a new commercial construct — 'Anchored Reserves with Scaled Surge Crediting' — that combines a predictable base reservation, a thin autoscale band with SLA tiers, and an anonymized, time-decayed surge credit pool that offsets overage costs during genuine traffic spikes. Objectives: 1) Reduce negotiation friction for mid-market/enterprise buyers by offering clearly defined SLOs and a deterministic overage remediation path. 2) Keep average effective unit cost within 10% of current reserved pricing for steady-state workloads. 3) Avoid large up-front commitments for customers with bursty seasonal traffic. Success metrics: - Conversion rate from trial to paid for Dedicated customers in pilot >= 25% - Average monthly overage credits consumed <= 15% of anchored reserve cost for pilot customers - SLA adherence: P99 tail latency targets met 99.8% of the time across pilot hosts Proposed packaging (pricing experiments): - Anchored Reserve (AR): customer commits to 60-80% of forecasted steady-state throughput (kGPU-hours) for a 12-month term. Anchored discount applies to AR usage. - Scaled Surge Band (SSB): an autoscaling allowance above AR, sized in elastic bands (small/medium/large) with soft SLA tiering. SSB has a higher per-unit charge but is paired with Surge Credits. - Surge Credit Pool (SCP): at contract start Redwood allocates surge credits equal to X% of AR value (experiment with 5%, 10%, 20%). Credits are consumed first for SSB usage before monetary overage billing. Unused credits decay quarterly at a 25% rate to keep behavior aligned to genuine spikes. Experiment variants: - Variant A (Conservative): AR=80% forecast, SCP=5% AR value, SSB rate = 1.8x AR unit price, SLA tier = standard (SLA rebate model) - Variant B (Balanced): AR=70% forecast, SCP=10%, SSB rate = 1.5x, SLA tier = premium (faster response, higher uptime) - Variant C (Aggressive adoption): AR=60% forecast, SCP=20%, SSB rate = 1.3x, SLA tier = premium + priority capacity routing Trade-offs considered: - Larger SCP increases customer comfort but reduces Redwood realized revenue and complicates forecasting. - Lower AR commitment improves sign-up conversion but shifts utilization risk to Redwood; needs stronger autoscale governance and preemption policies. - Surge credit decay reduces credit hoarding but introduces complexity in contract wording. Negotiation playbook (for AEs/CS): 1) Start with Variant B as baseline for mid-market; present Variant A when customer asks for higher predictability; offer Variant C as a strategic pilot for high-velocity AI startups. 2) During legal review call out: credit decay mechanics, reconciliation windows, and what constitutes force majeure for credit replenishment. 3) Use a 3-month lookback telemetry clause (customer-visible) to recommend AR sizing adjustments at renewal. Implementation notes (product & infra): - Billing: create a surfaced line item for SCP consumption; maintain credit ledger per account and exportable reconciliation CSV. - Console UX: add a Reserve + Surge summary card with estimated AR utilization, remaining SCP, and projected burn rate. - Runtime: autoscale bands must honor SLO routing; if capacity constrained, route to compatible model variants or fall back to hosted. - Observability: dashboard with AR vs SSB utilization, credit depletion timelines, and SLO breaches. Pilot plan: - Recruit 3 pilot customers: 1 AI-first startup, 1 mid-market SaaS, 1 regulated enterprise. - Duration: 3 months production pilot with monthly checkpoints. - Data collection: per-customer burn rate, effective unit cost, SLO adherence, CSAT. Legal/finance considerations: - Include explicit audit windows for credit consumption and reconciliation cadence. - Define refund mechanism or make-good credits for repeated SLA misses. - Tax and revenue recognition: treat SCP as deferred revenue allocated across 12 months with decay mechanics. Rollout criteria: - Conversion uplift >= 15% versus current reserved baseline OR average effective unit cost reduction vs. committed reserved price >= 8% for pilot cohort. Rollback criteria: - SCP consumption > 40% of AR value persistently across pilots without corresponding growth in paid AR within 2 consecutive months. Next steps: - Finalize PRD and contract language (owner: PM) - Align engineering for console and billing changes (owner: ENG) - Schedule legal deep-dive to lock decays and reconciliation windows (owner: Legal)
comments: 2025-11-03: Initial scoping meeting with ENG, Sales, Legal. Agreement to prototype credit ledger behavior in billing service.

2025-11-04: Engineering flagged risk: credit ledger must be strongly eventual-consistent; proposed debounce window for high-frequency job runs to avoid double-burn. Action: add rate limiter for credit consumption (ENG-assign).
2025-11-05: Sales feedback: AE requests an 'entry' variant with AR < 60% to convert smaller customers; added as Variant C for pilot.
2025-11-06: Finance note: defer revenue allocation approach to RevRec working group; need GAAP alignment before public pricing sheet.
2025-11-07: Design uploaded mockups for console card (Figma link in links). Design suggests showing forecast burn-through at current QPS.
2025-11-08: Legal reviewed credit decay language and requested explicit customer notification windows for decay events (30 days notice).
2025-11-10: PM decision: baseline pilot to use Variant B; begin contracting conversations with two anchor customers next week.
